newsitem.title: SPAIN: Clintons go yachting with royals off resort island.
newsitem.headline: Clintons go yachting with royals off resort island.

text.p: President Bill Clinton eased into a NATO-related European trip on Sunday with a dream holiday -- yachting with Spain's King Juan Carlos in the clear blue Mediterranean waters that bathe this craggy island resort.

Accompanied by his wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea, Clinton boarded the Fortuna, a sleek twin-turbine speedboat that Juan Carlos uses as his royal yacht, for a sun-splashed six-hour excursion along a scenic section of coastline studded with promontories and inlets. Also aboard the 85-foot yacht were Queen Sophia and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Anzar and his wife Ana Botella.
Clinton and Juan Carlos, in polo shirts and baseball caps, stood on the bridge waving to people in other boats as Fortuna slowly motored out of Palma harbour.

Among the vessels that cheered them on their way was the U.S.S. Hue City, an Aegis-class Navy cruiser. As the royal yacht passed the warship, Clinton returned a salute from American sailors lined up along the port rail.
Once out in open waters, Fortuna roared off to the northwest, trailing a wake that bespoke its speed of more than 30 knots, as a flotilla of security boats plunged along in its wake.

"The Clintons were very, very relaxed. They enjoyed it quite a bit," said White House spokesman Barry Toiv, who added that the king piloted the boat himself for most of the journey. Another White House official said he had never seen the U.S. first family more at ease.

After anchoring for lunch in the tiny port of Punta Andraitx, about 40 miles from Palma, the yachting party retraced their coastal cruise route, which took them past the site of the 800-year-old battle where Spain won Majorca from the Moors.

The waterborne fun was a prelude to the July 8-9 NATO summit in Madrid at which leaders of the 16-member alliance will start the process of expanding its sphere eastward into former communist Warsaw Pact states.

Clinton, who has made clear his determination to limit the first round of expansion to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic despite French pressure to add Slovenia and Romania as well, planned to arrive in Madrid on Monday afternoon for a series of meetings before the summit.
His summit-eve agenda included a meeting with U.S. lawmakers who, like parliamentarians from other member countries, must approve NATO expansion, and talks with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana.
